title: Memory bank affinity and kernel selection deep dive (TensorRT-LLM vs vLLM, CUDA graphs, VPC)
summary: Deep dive on GPU memory bank affinity, kernel path selection heuristics, and CUDA Graph stability comparing TensorRT-LLM and vLLM. Customer has a VPC/on-prem mix and is concerned about KV cache persistence under eviction and preemption. Agreed next steps: run 3-config microbench and share perf sheet; follow-up on private deployment options.
next_steps: Redwood to run 3-config benchmark on customer's 8x-A100-equivalent setup and upload perf sheet
Customer to provide 500-1k sample prompts and target latency SLOs
Schedule follow-up demo focused on private control plane + KMS integration
action_items: Diego Alvarez - kick off benchmark run and upload perf spreadsheet - 2026-05-12
Marcus Li - share sample prompt sets and production traffic histogram - 2026-05-08
Lina Park - send security overview, SOC2/ISO notes and TRTLLM tuning doc - 2026-05-07
transcript:
Meeting header: Date/Time: 2026-05-05 14:00 UTC | Duration: 82m | Attendees: Lina Park, Diego Alvarez, Marcus Li, Olivia Romero, Samir Patel

[00:00] Lina Park: Hey everyone thanks for joining. quick agenda: memory-bank affinity, kernel selection differences between TRT-LLM and vLLM, cuda graphs behavior under pinned vs pageable memory, and the VPC/onprem constraints you referenced. does that capture it?
[00:18] Marcus Li: yep that's it. we've been seeing weird tail latency spikes when we hit around 1.2k tokens with long contexts, and sometimes the KV cache seems to not be reused across small warmups.
[00:32] Diego Alvarez: thanks. before we dive, can you remind us of your infra? are you running multi-gpu with NVLink, or single-gpu nodes behind a shard router?
[00:45] Marcus Li: it's kinda hybrid. on-prem we have 4xA100 nodes with NVLink in a DGX-like config. cloud is 8xA100-equivalent instances but they're separate machines tied by our routing layer. VPC peering is used for control plane to the private nodes.
[01:03] Olivia Romero: and we need everything PCIe-blessed on prem because of compliance and no public internet to the inference box, so we can't do hosted mode.
[01:14] Lina Park: got it. so private deployment constraints matter. on the memory-affinity note: one common issue is that numa/hamilton? (sic) — NUMA binding for pinned memory can cause kernels to pick different execution paths. TRT-LLM's allocator is more aggressive with pinned HBM lifts, whereas vLLM tends to fall back to pageable allocations if it sees fragmentation.
[01:39] Samir Patel: when you say "execution paths" do you mean different kernel selection? like cuBLAS vs custom fused kernels?
[01:46] Diego Alvarez: exactly. small differences in pointer alignment and page locality can flip the heuristics in the runtime that choose a fused attention kernel vs a generic matmul. that changes both latency and the suitability for CUDA Graph capture.
[02:05] Marcus Li: that matches our logs, sometimes the kernel name changes mid-run and then our cudagraph replay fails with invalid launch.
[02:13] Lina Park: yeah, cudagraphs are brittle when a kernel switch happens at runtime because the captured sequence no longer matches. TRT-LLM often uses cudagraphs but with a more deterministic kernel choice because of its static fusing; vLLM can be more dynamic which helps quality but hurts graph stability.
[02:36] Olivia Romero: then is the recommendation to force a kernel path? how invasive is that?
[02:42] Diego Alvarez: there are a couple of levers: one is to pin memory and warm up with representative sequence lengths so the runtime sticks to a kernel. another is to use our "kernel pin" config which biases the mapper to a stable path (tradeoff: might slightly worsen p99 on some tails). we also have an eviction-aware batching layer that tries to keep KV cache hot.
[03:05] Marcus Li: what about quantization? we've considered int8 for cost but worried about stability and divergence between TRT-LLM and vLLM outputs.
[03:13] Lina Park: quantization will change kernel selection too — int8 fused kernels are different and may require extra transposes or fused dequantize ops. TRTLLM's int8 execution tends to be faster but requires per-channel calibration; vLLM supports q4/q8 paths but might take a different kernel path that isn't cudagraph-friendly. we recommend running quality-focused evals with the sample prompts you share.
[03:41] Samir Patel: the KV cache persistence issue — is that because of device memory fragmentation or because of our preemption on cloud instances?
[03:48] Diego Alvarez: both. if the process is preempted and the allocator returns fragmented pages, next run may reallocate and not reuse the same buffer addresses, causing the runtime to evict and rebuild KV cache. on top of that, if you rely on pageable memory the OS can relocate pages during OOM/eviction. pinned allocations + sticky allocator policies reduce that.
[04:14] Marcus Li: okay. what about the VPC part: we have a private control plane but we still need health checks and remote tracing. latency to control plane shouldn't affect token latency right?
[04:23] Lina Park: control plane calls are async and shouldn't impact per-token latency for steady-state generation. the main VPC impacts are: network latency for model downloads during deploy, policy routing for model variants across regions, and access to KMS for key unwrap. we covered key management docs earlier, I'll re-share.
[04:42] Olivia Romero: can you talk us through an actual bench config you'd run?
[04:46] Diego Alvarez: yes. our plan: three configs. (1) pinned memory + cudagraph capture + TRTLLM tuned kernels; (2) pageable memory + cudagraphs off + vLLM dynamic paths; (3) pinned memory + cudagraphs on + vLLM but with kernel-pin toggle. we instrument NVTX and perf counters and measure p50/p90/p99 latency, throughput, GPU util, and kernel-switch counts.
[05:12] Marcus Li: good. and artifacts?
[05:15] Lina Park: we'll upload a perf spreadsheet (link provided in follow-up). we'll also include a small NVTX trace you can open in nsight. note: cudagraph replay mismatches often show up as "invalid kernel launch" or "assert failure" in our logs — sample grep commands will be included.
[05:36] Samir Patel: any gotchas when running these on your private package vs our on-prem?
[05:41] Diego Alvarez: on-prem tends to be more deterministic since you can control drivers and driver+CUDA versions. cloud can introduce small driver diffs. also watch for MPS / MIG config if you run multiple tenants — MIG can change kernel choices too.
[06:00] Olivia Romero: can Redwood's optimize toolkit recommend batch sizes to avoid thrashing?
[06:05] Lina Park: yes, Optimize runs an automated sweep and recommends batching/kv-cache sizes. but for this case we want to run the manual microbench to surface kernel switching. after that Optimize can suggest final knobs.
[06:18] Marcus Li: curious — do you have an internal chart showing kernel-switch frequency vs tail latency?
[06:22] Diego Alvarez: yes i'll attach one. quick callout: kernel-switch events correlate strongly with p99 spikes in our internal logs, especially when sequence length distribution is bimodal.
[06:34] Lina Park: let's walk a bit through an example trace. (screen share) here's a run where we warm up with 128 tokens then hit a 1024 token path; you can see at 00:23 the runtime switched to a fused attention kernel and cudagraphs invalidated.
[06:52] Marcus Li: that explains our spikes. is the fix essentially to avoid the mid-run switch?
[06:56] Diego Alvarez: yes either avoid it by shaping workloads or stabilize by pinning kernels. if you cannot shape traffic, we recommend a hybrid fallback that captures small graphs for the hot path and falls back to slower paths for cold tails.
[07:12] Samir Patel: about the hybrid fallback — how do you measure the cost tradeoff? p50 vs cost per token?
[07:17] Lina Park: we break down cost as tokens * (compute ms per token) and run per-route estimates. hybrid adds complexity but often reduces p99 by 30-50% at a small p50 regress. we'll show numbers in the perf sheet.
[07:32] Olivia Romero: on the security side, we'll need KMS unwrapping locally for keys — does private deployment support HSM integration?
[07:39] Lina Park: yes, HSM and customer-managed KMS are supported in Private. we'll attach the integration guide.
[07:47] Marcus Li: any immediate blockers for us to start the benchmark?
[07:50] Diego Alvarez: we need your prompt set and a small VM/SSH jumpbox or access to a node to run the bench harness. otherwise Redwood can run it on an 8x-A100-equivalent cluster we manage but results might differ slightly vs your on-prem driver matrix.
[08:05] Marcus Li: we'll share prompts and a representative traffic histogram.
[08:09] Lina Park: great. i'll summarize next steps at the end.

[46:00] (longer silence and screen-sharing of NVTX traces, Diego talking through histograms — omitted)

[68:10] Diego Alvarez: quick note on cudagraph replay: if you get a mismatch, check for small floating point non-determinism and non-idempotent kernel selection due to different launch params. sometimes the kernel name is identical but a flag triggers a different internal code path. adding a deterministic seed and matching workspace sizes during warmup helps.
[69:05] Marcus Li: we saw a repro where changing batch-size from 4 to 5 flipped kernel choice, which was surprising.
[69:11] Lina Park: yep small batch-size boundaries often cross heuristics. Optimize can recommend stable bins.
[70:00] Olivia Romero: what should we expect in the perf sheet?
[70:05] Diego Alvarez: you'll get a table with p50/p90/p99, throughput (tokens/sec), GPU util, memory fragmentation metric, and kernel-switch count. each config will have a small trace and a link to NVTX.
[70:18] Marcus Li: timeline?
[70:21] Lina Park: Diego will start bench next week and upload by 2026-05-12, we should reconvene the week of 2026-05-18 for results and an on-prem deployment planning slot.
[70:34] Samir Patel: excellent. Olivia: any other security asks?
[70:38] Olivia Romero: just SOC2/ISO paperwork and KMS integration details, nothing blocking.
[70:44] Lina Park: perfect. quick recap and next steps: 1) Diego runs the 3-config bench and uploads perf sheet; 2) Marcus sends prompts and traffic histogram; 3) Lina shares SOC2/ISO + TRTLLM tuning notes and NVTX grep sample. we'll schedule a follow-up for the week of May 18.
[71:05] Marcus Li: sounds good thanks everyone.
[71:09] Olivia Romero: thank you.
[71:12] Diego Alvarez: thanks, bye.

Meeting ended: 15:22 UTC. Artifacts mentioned: perf spreadsheet (will be shared in follow-up), NVTX traces, TRTLLM tuning doc, SOC2/ISO notes.
